rows.see: how to know the agentic loop is done / when to terminate
rows.answer: Check the `stop_reason` field. Never use text presence, an iteration cap, or 'task complete' phrasing.

rows.see: prevent the agent returning text (force a tool)
rows.answer: Do not force `tool_choice:'any'` to stop text. That loops forever. Stop on `stop_reason`.

rows.see: reduce agent round-trips / Claude requests tools in separate sequential turns
rows.answer: Prompt Claude to **batch** tool requests per turn and return all tool results together before the next call. Not composite tools, speculative execution, or a bigger `max_tokens`.

rows.see: guard against a runaway loop burning tokens (bug / pathological input)
rows.answer: Keep `stop_reason` as the primary stop; add an **iteration cap** only as a *secondary* backstop. Never make the cap the primary signal.

rows.see: how the loop picks the next tool — planned sequence, decision tree, or status-field routing?
rows.answer: None of those. Each turn the model reasons over the results appended to the conversation and chooses the next action. The loop is **model-driven**, not a pre-planned tool sequence, a decision tree, or orchestration-layer routing on a status field.

rows.see: what to do with a tool result before the next call / why append it to history
rows.answer: Append it as a new message and resend the **whole** conversation — the Messages API is **stateless**, so the model only sees what its call returned (and reasons about the next step) if the full history is carried each turn. Not server-side session memory, an external-store reference id, or replacing the earlier message; not caching, dedup, or a role-alternation rule.

rows.see: `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` and the last content block is a cut-off `tool_use`
rows.answer: Truncated: not final and not runnable. **Discard** the partial call: don't execute it, don't splice a 'continue' onto it, don't treat it as `end_turn`. If the cap was set too low for a normal-sized answer, retry with a higher `max_tokens`. If the output is inherently too big (many files, modules, or items), **split into smaller scoped calls and merge** the results in code.

rows.see: several `tool_use` blocks in one response / one of the parallel calls failed or was skipped
rows.answer: Return **one `tool_result` per `tool_use` id, all in the next single user message**, with `tool_result` blocks before any text. The failed or skipped call still gets a result with `is_error: true`. Not one message per result, not omitting the failure, not a merged text summary.

rows.see: the tool call is still cut off after every `max_tokens` raise / the output grows with the number of files, modules, or items
rows.answer: The output is inherently too big for one response. **Split** it into smaller scoped calls (a few modules or files per call) and **merge** the resulting structures in code. Not another `max_tokens` raise up to the model's ceiling, not executing the partial `tool_use`, not a spliced 'continue'.

rows.see: make subagents talk to each other / share memory
rows.answer: No. Subagents are isolated. They talk only through the coordinator and inherit none of its history.

rows.see: independent tasks running one after another
rows.answer: Run them at the same time. Issue parallel Task calls in one response.

rows.see: coordinator already holds the findings, or a small single-file task alongside a large multi-file one
rows.answer: Delegate by size. The coordinator answers trivial or already-held work **directly**; it delegates only the large, scoped task to a subagent. Don't re-ingest what it already holds.

rows.see: parallel agents all working from the **original** code/data
rows.answer: Order by dependency. Run the **producer first**, then parallelize the now-independent consumers on its output. Not a shared memory store, not strict all-sequential.

rows.see: context filling / accuracy dropping mid-investigation across many files
rows.answer: Delegate scoped work to fresh-context `Explore` subagents that return a summary. Don't `/compact`, `/clear`, or `Grep` the main context to push on.

rows.see: two credible sources give directly conflicting values
rows.answer: Annotate both with source attribution and **defer** the choice to the coordinator. Never pick a winner by credibility heuristic, never pass both unflagged.

rows.see: synthesis flattens every source into one format (all bullets/JSON/prose)
rows.answer: Render **per content type** — tables for financial data, prose for news. Don't standardize to one format or add a common intermediate representation.

rows.see: query mix varies in complexity (simple fact vs deep comparative) and keeps evolving
rows.answer: Let the **coordinator** reason per query and invoke only the subagents it needs — a single web lookup skips the full pipeline. Beats a trained complexity classifier, fixed pattern-based routing, or a hardcoded fast-path.

rows.see: every subagent succeeded, yet the report misses whole sub-domains of the topic
rows.answer: Root cause is the **coordinator's task decomposition** being too narrow — the workers did exactly what they were assigned. Fix the decomposition, don't blame the downstream search/analysis/synthesis agents.

rows.see: colleague suggests agents send output directly to each other instead of routing through the coordinator
rows.answer: Keep the coordinator as the hub: it observes every interaction, handles errors consistently, and controls what each subagent receives. Not because serialization, request-batching, or retry logic is coordinator-only — those can live anywhere.

rows.see: both agents returned findings — now produce one integrated output
rows.answer: Coordinator passes **both** sets to the synthesis agent for unified integration. Concatenating raw outputs isn't integration; agents merging peer-to-peer or bypassing the coordinator breaks the hub.

rows.see: agents duplicate each other's work; token usage doubles without more coverage
rows.answer: Have the coordinator **partition the research space before delegating** — distinct subtopics/source types per agent (fixes the unclear boundaries at the source). Not shared-state focus logging, not dedupe-after, not dropping parallelism for sequential.

rows.see: coordinator tempted to do a large multi-file task itself to avoid subagent overhead
rows.answer: Loading dozens of files into one context **dilutes attention** — delegate to scoped subagents. The coordinator can write code and isn't rate-limited into blocking; the real cost is attention, not tools.

rows.see: cut latency on a big analysis — recursive agent hierarchy, self-spawning subagents, or an async worker-pool queue?
rows.answer: Coordinator spawns **flat parallel subagents** over subsets and aggregates. Avoid recursive hierarchies, letting subagents spawn their own subagents, or a message-queue pool — they lose the coordinator's single hub for monitoring and debugging.

rows.see: subagent can't see the coordinator's history / other outputs
rows.answer: Pass the full context in the prompt, metadata included. Nothing is shared for you.

rows.see: missing citations in the synthesis output
rows.answer: The cause is context passed without metadata, not the synthesis agent.

rows.see: coordinator talks about delegating but no subagent runs, and logs show no errors
rows.answer: The `Task` tool (renamed `Agent`) is missing from the coordinator's `allowedTools` — it can reason about delegating but has no tool to actually spawn a subagent. Not a `max_tokens` truncation or a missing-context issue.

rows.see: subagent given an exact step-by-step procedure (queries, source priorities, file/line edits) and won't adapt or recover
rows.answer: Delegate goals + quality criteria (coverage breadth, source diversity, recency), let the subagent pick its own approach. Rigid procedures block adaptation; bare goals with no criteria at all are the opposite failure.

rows.see: combined upstream outputs (e.g. 155K tokens) blow past the synthesis agent's optimal window
rows.answer: Fix it at the source: have upstream agents return structured data (key facts, citations, relevance scores) instead of verbose content and reasoning traces. A summarizer agent or a RAG store adds latency/cost or loses comprehensive coverage.

rows.see: configure AgentDefinitions for a coordinator plus specialists that each need different tools
rows.answer: One AgentDefinition per specialist with scoped tools (~4–5 each), and give the coordinator the `Task` tool to spawn them. Not one mega-agent holding every tool, not separate HTTP endpoints, not the coordinator doing everything itself.

rows.see: two independent subagents, want them to run concurrently to cut wall-clock time
rows.answer: Emit both `Task` calls within a single coordinator response — the SDK launches them concurrently. Separate turns run sequentially, there is no `parallel: true` flag on one Task call, and merging both jobs into one subagent defeats the purpose.

rows.see: Claude keeps suggesting tests/scenarios already covered in the existing suite
rows.answer: Include the existing test file in the context — the model can only reason about what it can see. Keyword-based post-filtering is brittle (misses renamed equivalents) and simply cutting the requested count doesn't help.

rows.see: coordinator spawns other subagents fine but never picks one specialist, and does that work itself
rows.answer: Rewrite that AgentDefinition's `description` to say what it handles and when to use it — Claude matches tasks against descriptions. The `prompt` field is the subagent's own system prompt, read only after it is spawned; `Task`/`Agent` in `allowedTools` is already working, and its `tools` list doesn't matter until it is spawned.

rows.see: subagent is spawned but can't do its job (guesses from file names, "can't open the file"), no errors, no permission prompts
rows.answer: Its AgentDefinition `tools` list omits the tool it needs — a tool left out is not in its session at all, so nothing errors. Add it to that `tools` list (omitting `tools` inherits every tool available to subagents). The coordinator's `allowedTools` does not give the subagent tools.

rows.see: handing off to a human
rows.answer: Carry every important field, like customer ID and recommended action. The human cannot see the transcript.

rows.see: a required tool order must hold every time (verify identity before `lookup_order`/`process_refund`, rollback script before `DROP`/`ALTER TABLE DROP`, synthesis before final report)
rows.answer: Add a **programmatic prerequisite gate** that blocks the later tool until the precondition returns success. A system prompt or few-shot 'always do X first' is probabilistic and cannot guarantee compliance when errors are costly. A routing classifier that enables a *subset* of tools fixes tool **availability**, not **ordering**.

rows.see: the test suite must pass before a task is marked complete, every time
rows.answer: A **Stop/PreToolUse hook** that blocks completion unless the test command exited `0` enforces it in code, outside the model. A CLAUDE.md line, a system-prompt line, and a `.claude/rules/` entry are all read by the model = probabilistic; `.claude/rules/` looks authoritative but is still just model-read.

rows.see: sessions end with neither a resolution nor an escalation / ticket closed or left open when the loop stops on the cap, the budget, or errors
rows.answer: Orchestrator **code** maps every exit path to one outcome: `end_turn` / `success` → resolution; `max_tokens` → retry with a higher cap if it was too low, or split inherently large output into smaller calls; cap hit, budget hit, or errors after retries → `escalate_to_human` with a structured handoff. Not a Stop hook, not a prompt rule, not raising or removing `max_turns`, not an unbounded rerun, not closing on any non-`tool_use` exit.

rows.see: Agent SDK result `error_max_turns` / `error_max_budget_usd` / `error_during_execution`
rows.answer: Check the **`subtype`** before reading `result`, which is present only on `success`. Every subtype still carries `session_id`, `total_cost_usd` and `num_turns`, so you can resume or hand off. Also wrap the call in try/catch: a single-shot `query()` raises after an error result, and a connection failure yields no result message.

rows.see: authorization state must survive a handoff between agent steps (verified identity, supervisor approval, refund cap)
rows.answer: Emit a **structured handoff record**: verified customer ID + how it was verified, the approver, the approved amount/order, what the next step may and may not do. **Gate** the next tool on those fields (the approved cap, not the agent's generic limit). A resumed session or a pasted transcript carries approvals only as prose the model reads.

rows.see: escalating to a human after the agent already acted (identity checked, a credit applied)
rows.answer: Customer ID, root cause, amount and recommended action are the floor. Also include the **authorization state**: verification status + method, actions already completed, and the amount still outstanding. Without it the human re-verifies or repeats the credit/refund.

rows.see: high-stakes compliance must not fail / drop to 0%
rows.answer: Use a hook. A stronger prompt, few-shot or routing can still fail, because the model can ignore text.

rows.see: block a policy-violating action before it runs
rows.answer: A PreToolUse hook. It blocks before. PostToolUse is too late, the action already ran.

rows.see: normalise / transform tool output consistently
rows.answer: A PostToolUse hook. It runs after. Do not ask the model to do it.

rows.see: a step must **run** after every subagent / tool call — the model can't be trusted to do it
rows.answer: A PostToolUse hook (e.g. on the `Task` tool) fires it deterministically after each call returns. A system prompt, a `CLAUDE.md` note or a few-shot transcript only nudges — the model may skip it.

rows.see: complex multi-part request balloons to 12+ tool calls with low resolution, investigating concerns sequentially and re-gathering the same customer data
rows.answer: **Decompose** into distinct concerns, **investigate in parallel** over shared customer context, then **synthesize** one resolution. Adding more verification gates/checkpoints makes the sequential problem worse; few-shot ideal sequences don't systematically fix context reuse or parallelism.

rows.see: coverage gaps in a multi-agent system / subagents missed things
rows.answer: Fix how the coordinator splits the work. Do not blame the subagents or add more of them.

rows.see: attention dilution / the model loses focus across many files
rows.answer: Split the work into passes, then add one pass that joins the batches. A bigger model or window does not fix it.

rows.see: open-ended investigation (research, debugging, impact or migration audit) — scope unknown until you look
rows.answer: **Dynamic decomposition**: the coordinator reads each result and generates the next subtasks from it (add, drop, re-scope). A fixed pipeline, a fixed pipeline plus a retry step, or an integration pass over the first step's matches cannot add the subtask a finding calls for.

rows.see: understand a large/unfamiliar codebase / where do I start reading (800+ files)?
rows.answer: `Grep` for entry points (login, token verify, middleware), read those, then follow imports and calls outward — map it **incrementally**. Do not read every file matching `auth`/`token`, and do not fan out subagents before you find an entry point.

rows.see: evaluate N independent items individually, then find patterns across the whole set (audit 50 tickets)
rows.answer: Map-reduce chain: a per-item pass scores each one on its own, then a **separate** synthesis pass over all the scores surfaces systemic patterns. Cramming all N into one pass loses per-item rigor; sampling a few and extrapolating skips the rest.

rows.see: a plan's later steps run "as planned" / "unchanged" even though an early step showed the premise or scope was wrong
rows.answer: The defect is the **fixed sequence**. The coordinator must review each result before choosing the next subtasks — e.g. add a subtask on why districts reversed a policy, or map how modules reach the database before reviewing them. Retrying the same step, caveating the report, or running the steps in parallel leaves the fixed plan in place.

rows.see: chain or adapt? a known file set with fixed review aspects vs a task whose next step depends on what you find
rows.answer: Can you list every step before step 1 runs, with no result that would change them? → **prompt chaining** (per-file passes + a cross-file integration pass). Otherwise → **dynamic decomposition**. An integration pass only covers what the fixed first step found, so it cannot rescue an open-ended audit; and don't pick adaptive for a predictable checklist review.

rows.see: `fork_session` vs `--resume`
rows.answer: `--resume` continues the same session. `fork_session` branches off to explore.

rows.see: only 3 of 50 files changed
rows.answer: Start a fresh session and inject a summary of the 3 files. Do not re-explore everything, and do not `--resume`, because its tool results are stale.

rows.see: a few of the files the session read were changed since (renamed / merged overnight)
rows.answer: `--resume` the session — keep the context you already built — and tell the agent exactly which files changed for targeted re-analysis. Don't re-read all files, don't start fresh: the rest of the context is still accurate.

rows.see: explore two approaches in parallel from the same analysis, without losing either
rows.answer: `fork_session` — branch from the shared baseline so each approach gets its own independent context and neither contaminates the other. Not sequential in one thread (cross-contamination), not two fresh sessions (needless re-analysis).

rows.see: resume one specific past session by name after working on other codebases since
rows.answer: `--resume <name>` loads that named session out of many. `--continue` only picks up the most **recent** conversation; `--session-id` needs the UUID from the transcript, not the name.

rows.see: context polluted with several failed / conflicting attempts; want a completely different strategy
rows.answer: Start a **fresh** session and inject a summary of what was tried and why each failed — keeps the lessons, drops the conflicting file modifications. Don't `fork_session` (it inherits the pollution), don't just tell it to 'ignore' the attempts.

rows.see: MCP server connected and healthy, but the agent keeps using a built-in (Grep, Write, `sed`) instead — MCP tool descriptions are one-liners
rows.answer: Enrich the MCP tool **descriptions** — capabilities, outputs, and when to prefer it. Selection is driven by the description the model sees, so a terse line loses to a built-in's rich one. Not removing the built-in, not a system-prompt router, not splitting into granular tools.

rows.see: the agent picks the wrong tool / misroutes
rows.answer: Improve the tool descriptions first. Claude picks tools from them, not from few-shot or a classifier.

rows.see: single-concern works (94%) but multi-concern tool selection drops (58%)
rows.answer: The model already knows the tools — add **few-shot** showing the multi-concern reasoning and tool sequence. Not a decompose preprocessing call, tool consolidation, or re-prompt validation.

rows.see: which few-shot examples fix ambiguous tool selection
rows.answer: **4-6** examples targeting the ambiguous cases, each with explicit comparative reasoning (why this tool over the alternative). Not 10-15 unambiguous or tool-grouped examples.

rows.see: a destructive tool must NEVER run without approval (hard guarantee)
rows.answer: A `PreToolUse` hook blocks the call outside the model. A tool description, system-prompt rule, or `few-shot` example only makes it likely, never certain.

rows.see: one generic tool with a free-text instruction, or one tool spanning several distinct operations (parameter confusion)
rows.answer: **Split** into purpose-specific tools, each with a defined input/output contract. Not an `operation_type` enum on the one tool, not richer descriptions/examples, not an internal routing layer.

rows.see: descriptions are well-written/unchanged, but a system-prompt phrase matching a tool name (`account`, `analyse content`, `refund`) steers the wrong tool
rows.answer: Keyword-sensitive prompt instruction forms an unintended association that overrides the descriptions. Rewrite the prompt to remove the keyword overlap / state the precise conditions. Not more description detail, few-shot, renaming, or fine-tuning.

rows.see: two tools across agents share terminology (both described as 'analyze …') → coordinator misroutes
rows.answer: Rename the colliding tool so the shared term (`analyze`) is gone, eliminating the overlap — don't just describe around it. Adding detail to one description only, a pre-routing classifier, or few-shot leaves the semantic overlap intact.

rows.see: a tool failed — how should the agent recover
rows.answer: Return structured error fields: `errorCategory`, `isRetryable`, `description`. Then the agent can pick the right recovery.

rows.see: MCP tool hits a backend error (order not found, DB failure) — how to report it
rows.answer: Put the message in the `content` field and set `isError: true`; Claude sees the failure flag **plus** readable text to reason on. Not a success wrapper with a `status` field, a thrown exception, or a silent empty result.

rows.see: which category for a business-rule failure (amount exceeds order total, non-returnable item)
rows.answer: `errorCategory: "validation"`, `isRetryable: false` — a permanent policy failure. Not `transient` (retries uselessly) or `permission` (wrong cause).

rows.see: empty result from a *successful* query
rows.answer: Return it explicitly — `isError: false`, empty array, a 'no results' message. Not a retry, not an error, and not a silent empty array (ambiguous).

rows.see: the agent has too many tools (e.g. 18) / unreliable selection
rows.answer: Give each agent about 4 or 5 tools for its own role. Split the tools that cross roles.

rows.see: structured output is required
rows.answer: Use a `tool_choice` that forces a call. `'auto'` can return text instead.

rows.see: a mandatory step must run first (e.g. extract metadata before enrichment)
rows.answer: Force `tool_choice: {"type":"tool","name":...}` on the first turn only, then hand back to `'auto'`. Reordering the tools array or `'any'`+prompt is probabilistic; forcing it on *every* call blocks the later steps.

rows.see: must call a tool but which one depends on input you can't know in advance
rows.answer: Use `tool_choice: "any"` — it forces a tool call but lets the model pick which. Forcing one specific tool is wrong when the type varies; `'auto'`+instruction still permits a text reply.

rows.see: a subagent goes outside its specialization / calls another agent's tools
rows.answer: Restrict its `allowedTools` to its own tools — a hard config-level limit it cannot bypass. A system-prompt rule or lower temperature is probabilistic and gets ignored.

rows.see: a general-purpose tool gets misused for the wrong job (e.g. `fetch_url` used to search)
rows.answer: Replace it with a narrower tool that validates/constrains at the interface (e.g. `load_document`), making the misuse impossible. A prompt caveat or domain blocklist only discourages and needs endless upkeep.

rows.see: a specialized agent keeps round-tripping to the coordinator for one simple cross-role need
rows.answer: Give it a scoped tool for the common case, keep complex cases routed through the coordinator (least privilege). Don't hand it the full toolset — that degrades its primary task.

rows.see: MCP available to the whole team
rows.answer: Commit a project `.mcp.json`. `~/.claude.json` is personal to one user.

rows.see: a standard integration (e.g. Jira)
rows.answer: Use the standard MCP server that already exists. Do not build your own.

rows.see: secrets in the MCP config
rows.answer: Use env-var expansion `${VAR}`. Never commit credentials.

rows.see: two same-named MCP tools collide (e.g. prod + staging `query_postgres`); agent calls the wrong one on a context-free prompt
rows.answer: Rename the personal tool to a distinct id in `~/.claude.json`, put the **environment** in its description, **and** add an explicit session routing instruction. Description tuning alone cannot route a prompt with no environment cue.

rows.see: agents make many exploratory tool calls just to discover what documentation/data is available before their real search
rows.answer: Expose a **content catalog as an MCP resource** — a browsable hierarchy of topics/summaries the agent reads once. Not caching exploratory results, raising `max_tokens`, or pre-loading every summary into the system prompt.

rows.see: `claude mcp add` printed `Added …` but the tools don't show up / Claude falls back to built-ins
rows.answer: `Added` only means the config was written. Check `claude mcp list`, `claude mcp get <name>` or `/mcp` for **Connected / Needs authentication / Failed to connect / Pending approval** and the tool count before tuning descriptions or CLAUDE.md.

rows.see: a `${VAR}` in the shared `.mcp.json` is unset on one developer's machine
rows.answer: The server **still loads** with the literal `${VAR}` text and a missing-variable warning in `claude mcp list` and `/mcp`, so auth fails. The developer sets the variable in their own environment. Never inline the token or commit a secret `:-default`. (Covered credential names like `NPM_TOKEN` in remote `url`/`headers` read as empty, no warning.)

rows.see: the same MCP server name defined in more than one scope
rows.answer: Not merged: **local > project > user**, and the whole entry from the winning scope is used. A `--scope user` copy of a project server is shadowed by `.mcp.json`.

rows.see: find where a function is called / search file *contents*
rows.answer: Grep searches file contents. Glob matches paths.

rows.see: find files by name / extension pattern
rows.answer: Glob matches paths. Grep searches contents.

rows.see: modify a file
rows.answer: Try Edit first. If the match is not unique, add more surrounding context before you fall back to Read plus Write.

rows.see: rename a variable / change **every** occurrence of a string in one file
rows.answer: `Edit` with `replace_all: true` — one operation. Not repeated Edits, not Read plus Write, not `sed`.

rows.see: Edit fails — the target is identical / repeated boilerplate, no context can make it unique
rows.answer: Read the whole file, modify in memory, then Write it back. A longer `old_string` or a bigger 'context window' cannot disambiguate identical sections.

rows.see: find all callers of a function exposed under renamed wrappers / aliases
rows.answer: Read the library and wrapper modules to collect every exposed name, then Grep each one. Grepping only the original name misses renamed callers.

rows.see: do all tool definitions load at connection time?
rows.answer: No. With tool search on (the default) only names and server instructions load. Full schemas load on demand.

rows.see: load all schemas upfront, zero on-demand latency (small trusted set)
rows.answer: Set `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false`. Unset or `=true` **defers** (tool search on).

rows.see: `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto`
rows.answer: Loads schemas upfront **only if** they fit within ~10% of the context (`auto:N` sets the %), else defers. Not 'always'.

rows.see: MCP protocol order over a connection
rows.answer: `initialize` (capabilities) → discovery at connect (`tools/list`, `resources/list`, `prompts/list`) → `tools/call` on demand → `list_changed` when the set changes. Discovery never precedes `initialize`.

rows.see: expose read-only data
rows.answer: Use a resource, which the app controls. A tool makes the model call it just to look around.

rows.see: many objects share the same shape
rows.answer: Use one templated resource URI, like `db://tables/{name}/schema`. Do not add one resource per object.

rows.see: pick the primitive: write op / read-only data / user-triggered workflow
rows.answer: tool (model-controlled) / resource (app-controlled, read-only) / prompt (user-controlled slash command). Match each to who initiates.

rows.see: shared with team / all developers / no manual setup
rows.answer: Put it in the project `.claude/…` folder and commit it to git.

rows.see: a new hire gets no instructions, same repo
rows.answer: The instructions sit in the personal `~/.claude/` folder, which git never shares. Move them into the project.

rows.see: first diagnostic step — works for one dev, not another
rows.answer: Run `/memory`. It shows which files really loaded.

rows.see: guarantee / always / at every save / regardless of what Claude does
rows.answer: Use a hook. It is a script that runs on an event. Never CLAUDE.md, a rule, or 'mark as important'.

rows.see: two rules conflict, must always hold
rows.answer: Use a hook or `settings.json`. CLAUDE.md has no hard precedence.

rows.see: CLAUDE.md has grown to 400–500 lines, all mixed together
rows.answer: Split it. Use `@import` for separate files, or a `.claude/rules/` folder by topic.

rows.see: which mechanism for which rule — hard block vs path-only convention vs soft preference
rows.answer: Match the type: a **hard constraint** → `settings.json` permission or a **PreToolUse** hook; a **path-scoped convention** → a `.claude/rules/` file with a glob; a **soft preference** the model may override → `CLAUDE.md`. Don't put a hard block in prose or a soft preference behind a hook.

rows.see: agent still reads forbidden paths (secrets / `.env`) despite a CLAUDE.md ban
rows.answer: Prevent it: a `deny` permission or a **PreToolUse** hook on `Read` refuses the access regardless of the model. A **PostToolUse** log only detects after the read; strengthening the prose keeps it model-followed; `context: fork` isolates conversation, not the filesystem.

rows.see: CLAUDE.md mixes hard prohibitions (never edit X / never read `.env`) with style guidance — how do you restructure it?
rows.answer: Split each line by *must it hold if Claude ignores it?* Hard prohibitions → `permissions.deny` (e.g. `Edit(db/migrations/**)`, `Read(**/.env)`) in the **committed** `.claude/settings.json`. Logic or fixed-point actions → a **hook**. Style and judgement guidance stays in `CLAUDE.md`, which is context, not enforced configuration.

rows.see: a team-wide block, but the deny sits in `.claude/settings.local.json`
rows.answer: Wrong file: `settings.local.json` is **personal**, so new clones don't get it. Team rules go in the committed `.claude/settings.json` (or managed settings).

rows.see: a narrower allow rule / `--allowedTools` / hook 'allow' to get past a broad deny
rows.answer: Doesn't work. Rules evaluate **deny → ask → allow**, a deny at any level wins, and an allow can't carve an exception out of it. A hook `allow` doesn't bypass a deny either. Instead, replace the broad deny with a **PreToolUse** hook that blocks every case except the permitted one; a blocking hook beats an allow rule.

rows.see: a file needed for **this task only**
rows.answer: Reference it in the prompt with `@path/to/file`, which includes the file's full content. Not CLAUDE.md or an `@import` (those load every session for everyone), and not a prose description of where the file lives.

rows.see: `@src/some-dir/`, expected to load the whole folder
rows.answer: `@directory` gives a **file listing, not contents**. Reference the files themselves with `@path` to include their content.

rows.see: context re-explained every session / the whole team needs it vs a one-off constraint
rows.answer: Reusable and cross-session → **CLAUDE.md** (or `@import` an existing doc; imports organise but don't reduce context). One-off → say it **inline** in the prompt.

rows.see: available to the whole team (command / skill)
rows.answer: Put it in `.claude/commands/` or `.claude/skills/` and commit it.

rows.see: personal, without affecting teammates
rows.answer: Put it in your personal `~/.claude/…` folder.

rows.see: noisy output / exploration clutters the conversation / keep the full analysis
rows.answer: Use `context: fork`. The skill runs in its own context and only the summary comes back.

rows.see: a rule must ALWAYS apply automatically
rows.answer: Not a skill. A skill runs only when someone invokes it. Use a hook.

rows.see: context useful only for one specific task, not every session (exemplar code for new endpoints; a PR-review / deploy / migration workflow)
rows.answer: Put it in a **skill** — loaded on-demand only when invoked. Not project CLAUDE.md (loaded every session, wastes context on unrelated work) and not `.claude/rules/` (location-based — still loads for other work in that path). Keep only the *universal* standards in CLAUDE.md.

rows.see: a coding standard/convention must apply automatically on **every** edit, no manual step (all TypeScript uses named exports)
rows.answer: Define it in project CLAUDE.md or `.claude/rules/` — always loaded, so it applies with no invocation. A skill or slash command needs manual/on-demand invocation, so it can't be relied on to always run. (A hook is for a hard deterministic *guarantee*, not a loaded convention.)

rows.see: one skill, three issues at once — invoked without args, bleeds unrelated conversation context, has broad/destructive tool access
rows.answer: Three skill frontmatter features, one per issue: `argument-hint` (prompts for the parameter), `context: fork` (isolates from conversation history), `allowed-tools` (restricts tool access). SKILL.md *instructions* to 'request a name / ignore prior context / avoid forbidden ops' don't enforce — skills are prompt templates, not programs. Splitting the skill doesn't isolate context either.

rows.see: your personal copy of a shared skill uses the **same name** (`/commit`) — will it override the team's?
rows.answer: No. Create the personal skill in `~/.claude/skills/` with a **different name** (`/my-commit`). A same-name personal skill is overridden — project `.claude/skills/` **takes precedence** over `~/.claude/`. There is no `override` flag and no username-conditional frontmatter.

rows.see: conventions for one file type scattered across 50+ folders (.tf, SQL, Java)
rows.answer: Use `.claude/rules/` with a glob, like `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]`.

rows.see: …rather than a CLAUDE.md in every folder
rows.answer: Yes, the glob is better. One place, it loads by itself, and it saves context.

rows.see: format/lint on **every** file Claude edits, deterministically (not 'usually')
rows.answer: A `PostToolUse` hook runs the formatter/linter/validator on the **completed** file; CLAUDE.md, `.claude/rules`, and few-shot only nudge the model.

rows.see: **never** write to a path (e.g. `/secrets`), **no exceptions**
rows.answer: A `permissions.deny` rule (static path match) or a `PreToolUse` hook that **denies** the write before the tool runs (when it needs logic) — the hard blocks; read-instructions can be ignored.

rows.see: conventions moved into `.claude/rules/`, but they still load in every session
rows.answer: The file has no `paths` frontmatter, so it loads at launch like `.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Add a glob such as `paths: ["**/*.tf"]`. An `@import` in CLAUDE.md won't help: imported files still load at launch.

rows.see: when does it apply — only for one task / on matching files / after every edit / never?
rows.answer: On demand for one task → a **skill**. When Claude works with matching files → a `.claude/rules/` file **with** `paths`. On every matching event → a **hook** (`PostToolUse` for the finished file, not `PreToolUse`). Must never happen → `permissions.deny` or a blocking `PreToolUse` hook. Always, as advice → `CLAUDE.md`.

rows.see: multi-file / architecture / migration of 30–60 files
rows.answer: Use plan mode. Plan first, then build.

rows.see: single-file fix, clear stack trace, one `if`
rows.answer: Just do it. Plan mode is too heavy here.

rows.see: new to the domain / requirements unclear
rows.answer: Let Claude ask questions first to close the gap.

rows.see: design first, then implement
rows.answer: Plan first, then execute directly.

rows.see: isolate noisy code exploration
rows.answer: Use a subagent. It keeps the noise in its own context.

rows.see: explore/investigate/audit in plan mode, then apply the fix you found — one session or split it?
rows.answer: Stay in one session: **plan mode** for the investigation/audit, then **switch to direct execution** to apply the changes. Don't keep plan mode running through the mechanical per-file edits, and don't fragment into separate `allowedTools`/new-session phases.

rows.see: several valid implementation approaches with different architectural implications **and** the ticket is vague on which to use
rows.answer: Enter **plan mode** to explore the options and present a recommendation before coding. Don't start direct execution on an assumed approach, and don't scaffold before the method is chosen — auth, error handling, and future capabilities differ per approach.

rows.see: same edit across many similar files must stay **consistent** (terminology, wording); ad hoc direct execution already drifted
rows.answer: Use **plan mode** first to fix a shared strategy — terminology glossary, section template, update order — before touching files. A single long session's context won't hold consistency on its own, and a hardcoded find-and-replace command is too rigid.

rows.see: small change, but **irreversible / external** (DB migration, deploy, data rewrite via Bash): "just rewind if it's wrong"
rows.answer: Still **plan and review first**. Checkpoints track only Claude's file edits, not Bash or external processes, and a git commit reverts code, not data.

rows.see: approach must be **approved by others before** implementation
rows.answer: **Plan mode**: Claude writes the plan without editing source. Share it, get their go-ahead, then approve and execute. Not a draft PR after coding, and not approving your own plan and executing.

rows.see: Claude reads the description differently each time
rows.answer: Give 2 concrete examples, which is few-shot. Do not rewrite the prose again.

rows.see: complex transform with many edge cases
rows.answer: Give Claude failing tests first. This is TDD.

rows.see: edits are independent of each other
rows.answer: Give them one at a time.

rows.see: edits affect each other
rows.answer: Give them all in one message.

rows.see: renders wrong but **no console error or exception**, source looks fine
rows.answer: Send a **screenshot** of the broken state plus repro steps. The defect is only in the render, so do not paste the source or describe pixels in prose.

rows.see: new to the domain, unsure which requirements even apply
rows.answer: Use the **interview pattern** — have Claude ask clarifying questions before proposing a design. Not examples or plan mode: you don't yet know the constraints to specify or rank.

rows.see: Claude keeps breaking a CLAUDE.md rule (e.g. mocks the DB despite an 'integration tests' rule)
rows.answer: Tighten the CLAUDE.md rule itself with concrete criteria + an example structure. Root cause is a vague instruction, not a missing enforcer — don't add a hook, subagent, or `.claude/rules/` file to police it.

rows.see: the `claude` script hangs / waits for input
rows.answer: Add the `-p` flag. It runs without a prompt.

rows.see: need machine-readable review findings for auto-comments
rows.answer: Use `--output-format json` plus `--json-schema '<schema>'`, and read the findings from `structured_output`. JSON alone still leaves the findings as free text in `result`.

rows.see: reviewing its own code in the same session
rows.answer: Do not do that. Use a separate, independent Claude run for the review.

rows.see: re-review after new commits, don't duplicate comments
rows.answer: Save the earlier findings (e.g. the `--json-schema` JSON as a workflow artifact) and put them in the next fresh `-p` run's prompt: report only **new or still-unaddressed** issues. Not `--resume` of the old review session (it brings back stale reads of the pre-fix code), not a path+line filter (lines shift), not a diff-only scope (misses breakage in untouched files).

rows.see: each CI run must **never overspend** a dollar limit
rows.answer: Use `--max-turns N` plus `--max-budget-usd X` — `--max-budget-usd` stops the run mid-flight. A post-hoc `total_cost_usd` check only detects overspend.

rows.see: two CI steps: one needs structured JSON, the other plain text
rows.answer: Add `--output-format json` only to the step whose output is parsed; leave the other on default text, and run each as its own `-p` invocation. Don't force JSON on both, and don't share one session with different prompts.

rows.see: a CI review stage keeps reporting categories another stage already covers / exclusions must apply on every run
rows.answer: Write the review criteria, accepted patterns and skip categories in the repository's **CLAUDE.md**, which Claude reads on every run. A custom `with:` input or a job env var never reaches the model. A filter job after the review only hides findings, and it deletes real bugs that were mislabelled.

rows.see: CI review runs shell commands / edits files it does not need (broad `--allowedTools` grant)
rows.answer: Narrow `--allowedTools` in `claude_args` to what the review needs (e.g. only `mcp__github_inline_comment__create_inline_comment`). Read-only tools need no grant, and in automation mode Claude has no shell or GitHub API access until granted. Not a CLAUDE.md 'never run shell' rule (text only influences), not the job's GitHub `permissions` block (scopes the token, not Claude's tools), not a cleanup step afterwards.

rows.see: CI review skips the team's criteria that a developer's laptop applies
rows.answer: The criteria sit in a personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (or a gitignored `CLAUDE.local.md`), and the runner only has committed files. Move them into the project `CLAUDE.md`. Copying the personal file onto the runner only patches it. `--bare` skips every CLAUDE.md, so leave it off this job.

rows.see: CI review job **edits files or runs commands** it shouldn't
rows.answer: Allowlist what the review needs: `--permission-mode dontAsk --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob,Bash(git diff *)"`. Any other call that would prompt is denied. A prompt line only asks, and `--disallowedTools "Edit" "Write"` still leaves Bash open.

rows.see: unattended CI run must edit files and run one command, **nothing else**
rows.answer: `-p --permission-mode dontAsk --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(npm test *)"`. Allow rules do nothing under `--dangerously-skip-permissions` (containers only). `acceptEdits` doesn't approve `npm test`. `auto` lets a classifier approve other commands.

rows.see: generated tests only check `toBeDefined` or that a mock was called
rows.answer: Write criteria into `CLAUDE.md`: each test asserts a specific outcome for a given input, and existence-only or mock-call-only checks don't count. Name the fixtures to use. A coverage gate, a vague "write meaningful tests" line, or a reviewer without criteria won't fix it.

rows.see: add one or two rules, keep normal Claude
rows.answer: Use `--append-system-prompt`. It adds to the normal prompt.

rows.see: the root persona is wrong (e.g. a release-notes generator starts running tests)
rows.answer: Use `--system-prompt`. It replaces the prompt completely.

rows.see: same, but text from a file
rows.answer: Use the `…-file` variants of the same flags.

rows.see: skip ALL auto-load (CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, MCP) — fast repeated calls
rows.answer: Use `--bare`.

rows.see: use ONLY the MCP from this config, drop the rest
rows.answer: Use `--strict-mcp-config`.

rows.see: too many false positives in review
rows.answer: Write explicit criteria: exactly what to flag and what to skip, plus code examples. Not 'be conservative', and not a confidence threshold.

rows.see: severity ratings inconsistent across runs / prose like 'critical means dangerous'
rows.answer: Replace prose descriptions with concrete code examples per severity level (critical/major/minor). Not an issue-type→severity **map** (loses code-path context), not proportional 'rate relative to this PR', not `temperature=0`, not a second reconciliation pass.

rows.see: vague instruction like 'check comments are accurate and up-to-date'
rows.answer: Define the exact target the model must test (e.g. flag a comment only when its claimed behavior contradicts the actual code). Explicit criteria beats **few-shot examples** here — examples only pattern-match what's shown and won't generalize to novel cases.

rows.see: one category's false-positive rate is killing trust in ALL findings
rows.answer: Temporarily disable the noisy category and keep the high-precision ones running while you refine its prompt with explicit criteria + code examples. Not a uniform strictness cut (harms the good categories), not showing confidence scores (still noisy, distrust persists), not leaving it on while slowly adding examples (trust keeps eroding — urgency).

rows.see: false positives on patterns this project deliberately accepts / exclusions must hold for every review
rows.answer: Put project conventions, accepted patterns and exclusion criteria in **persistent context** (CLAUDE.md, or the reviewer's system prompt) so every review gets them. Not a one-off PR reply or a single run's prompt line, not 'be conservative', not a keyword post-filter.

rows.see: inconsistent output formatting / detailed instructions didn't work
rows.answer: Add few-shot examples with the reasoning shown. That works better than more instructions.

rows.see: compound phrases split inconsistently, implied items appear, wildly varying entry counts
rows.answer: Add few-shot examples that demonstrate the interpretation (split rules, explicit-only, granularity). Beats enriching the schema or adding min/max count constraints — the problem is what *counts* as an entry, not the output shape.

rows.see: same field extracted in varied formats (`cotton blend` vs `Cotton/Polyester mix`), sometimes omitted
rows.answer: Few-shot examples showing the canonical format fix the drift and also raise recall on skipped values. `temperature=0` only removes randomness, not format inconsistency; a stronger model tier or a required field won't teach the target shape.

rows.see: valid JSON but empty/null required fields — info is present but in varied source layouts (inline citations vs bibliography)
rows.answer: Few-shot examples spanning the format distribution raise recall on the misses. Beats retry logic, regex post-processing, or making the field optional — those hide or patch the misses instead of teaching the model to recognize the varied structures.

rows.see: model fabricates values when the source uses informal wording (`spacious`, `generous open-plan`)
rows.answer: Few-shot examples that return `null` for informal descriptions and extract only explicit values teach the stated-vs-unstated boundary, cutting fabrication without hurting recall. Beats an 'only if highly certain' instruction, required-field validation, or dropping the field.

rows.see: few-shot agent correctly handles a case in a language none of the examples used
rows.answer: Few-shot conveys the underlying judgment criteria, which generalize to structurally similar, previously unseen cases — not literal token/pattern matching, memorized language-specific rules, or decomposition into example tokens.

rows.see: findings aren't auditable, no way to measure precision per rule
rows.answer: Add a structured `detected_pattern` enum naming the rule that fired (plus a detail field). Free-text reasoning or separate reasoning logs aren't queryable at scale, and more severity tiers add granularity without telling you which rule fired.

rows.see: cut investigation time, but findings must not be filtered before review
rows.answer: Require **reasoning + confidence inline** with each finding. Don't surface high-confidence only or suppress false-positive signatures (that filters pre-review); re-tiering blocking vs suggestion doesn't cut per-finding investigation time.

rows.see: guarantee a tool call / structured output
rows.answer: `tool_choice:'any'` forces a call. `'auto'` can return text.

rows.see: does a JSON schema prevent all extraction errors?
rows.answer: No. A schema stops syntax errors only. You still validate that the values are right.

rows.see: the model fabricates values when the source lacks info
rows.answer: Make the fields optional or nullable. Do not require every field.

rows.see: automate / parse Claude Code CLI review output in CI (inline PR comments)
rows.answer: CLI flags `--output-format json` + `--json-schema` enforce parseable structured findings. Prompt or `CLAUDE.md` formatting is followed inconsistently — unusable for automation.

rows.see: model writes a text analysis instead of calling the tool, or routes to the wrong tool
rows.answer: Instruction text overlaps the tool name (`check the security` ↔ `check_security`). Fix: **distinct, non-overlapping terminology** for instructions vs tool names/descriptions — not `tool_choice`, not longer descriptions.

rows.see: guarantee always-valid JSON with a fixed field set, not merely 'usually parseable'
rows.answer: A `tool_use` input schema constrains output to the declared shape. Prompt directives, few-shot examples, and self-check only raise the odds — and semantic correctness still needs separate validation.

rows.see: an enum keeps failing validation as new categories keep appearing
rows.answer: Add an `"other"` value plus a free-text detail field — keeps clean joins for the common cases with a typed escape hatch. Beats a free-form string, endlessly expanding the enum, or few-shot mapping to the nearest value.

rows.see: source formatting is inconsistent (prices, units, dietary tags)
rows.answer: Strict output schema **plus** explicit normalization rules in the prompt — extract and normalize in one pass. Beats normalizing in post-processing code, multi-attempt voting, or a separate call per field.

rows.see: fields are already nullable but the model still invents plausible values for absent info
rows.answer: Add a prompt instruction to return `null` for any field not directly stated in the source. The schema is fine — a stronger model tier or a second-LLM verifier is overkill.

rows.see: prefill the assistant turn to force JSON / pick a structured-output method for strict schema compliance
rows.answer: Use `tool_use` + a JSON schema (`tool_choice:'any'` or a named tool) — that guarantees the shape. Response prefilling and prompt-based formatting only steer the opening tokens, enforce no schema, and a prefill can't run while `tool_choice` forces a tool.

rows.see: strip a chatty preamble / control the first tokens, no schema needed
rows.answer: Prefill the assistant turn with the answer's opening — the model continues from there, no preamble. Forcing `tool_use` is overkill with no schema to enforce; a prompt instruction is followed inconsistently; temperature doesn't control structure.

rows.see: a large structured result (findings for every file, every line item) comes back cut off mid-array with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`
rows.answer: **Split** the task into smaller scoped calls with the same schema (per file batch / section / record batch) and **merge** the arrays in code (dedupe on a key, check every chunk returned). Not `max_tokens` at the model's ceiling, not trimmed fields or shorter findings, not keeping the items that arrived.

rows.see: extraction output truncates although the document fits the context window — switch to a larger-context model?
rows.answer: No. The input already fits; the limit being hit is the output (`max_tokens` / the model's maximum output), a separate limit from the context window. Split the extraction per section and merge the results.

rows.see: extraction failed — retry
rows.answer: Send the original document, the failed extraction and the exact error. A blind retry repeats the mistake.

rows.see: the information is genuinely absent
rows.answer: A retry cannot invent it. Retries fix format and structure, never missing data.

rows.see: sum of line items doesn't match the extracted total (OCR or extraction errors)
rows.answer: Add a `calculated_total` the model sums alongside the `stated_total`, and flag mismatches for human review — the discrepancy becomes a first-class signal. Proportionally adjusting the numbers hides the error instead of catching it.

rows.see: retries keep failing only on unfamiliar-language / capability cases
rows.answer: Apply the retry boundary: retry format errors (empty field, wrong shape) on analysable inputs, but route capability gaps to human review. More attempts, a bigger prompt, or 'try harder' can't create understanding the model lacks.

rows.see: cut cost — move everything to batch
rows.answer: Use the Batch API only where waiting is fine. Keep real-time and multi-turn flows synchronous. Batch costs 50% less and can take up to 24 hours.

rows.see: identical shared prefix on every request — cut cost
rows.answer: One `cache_control` breakpoint at the **end of the shared prefix** (system prompt, tool/schema, few-shot). Prefix-match only, so variable per-document content stays after it. `1h` TTL extends the idle window (write premium), it does **not** guarantee a hit.

rows.see: some batch items failed (e.g. `context_length_exceeded`) — how to reprocess?
rows.answer: Resubmit **only the failed items**, found by their `custom_id`, chunking the oversized docs then merging the partial extractions. Don't rerun the whole batch, bump `max_tokens`, or jump a model tier — that pays for the successes again and often fixes the wrong cause.

rows.see: iterative tool-calling / two-step pipeline (run one tool, then a second with its result) — move to batch?
rows.answer: You can't. Batch is fire-and-forget: it **supports** tool definitions and emits tool calls, but **cannot execute a tool and feed the result back mid-request**. The real blocker is the asynchronous model — not a missing feature, and not the 24h latency.

rows.see: match each batch result back to its original request / PR
rows.answer: Set `custom_id` per request to your identifier and match results by it. Not result ordering (not guaranteed), not parsing the content, not one-item-per-batch via batch ID.

rows.see: how often to submit / what batch window meets an N-hour SLA?
rows.answer: Worst case = your submit interval + up to 24h processing. Pick the interval so interval + 24h clears the SLA with cushion (e.g. every 4h → 28h worst case under a 30h SLA). A single end-of-day batch blows the window for early-arriving docs.

rows.see: about to run a new/untested prompt over thousands of docs
rows.answer: Test on a representative **20–50 doc sample**, refine, then submit the full batch. A flawed prompt otherwise fails all N at full cost; splitting into sub-batches or wrapping each request in a retry loop validates the prompt no earlier than one sample would.

rows.see: review its own code in the same session
rows.answer: Use a separate instance with no prior context. In the same session the model keeps its own reasoning and will not question it.

rows.see: large multi-file review
rows.answer: Review each file in its own pass, then add one pass across files. One big pass or a bigger-context model does not fix it.

rows.see: one prompt reviews security + business logic + API design; tuning one concern's examples lowers another's recall
rows.answer: Split into **per-concern passes**: one prompt with its own few-shot examples for each concern, then merge the findings. Not balancing the examples in the same prompt, not a verification pass (it removes false positives, it cannot recover missed findings), not per-file passes, not a bigger model or context window.

rows.see: split the review per file or per concern?
rows.answer: Go by the symptom. Depth drops on later files, or the same code gets contradictory verdicts → **per-file** passes plus a cross-file pass. One category's recall falls when another is tuned, even on small PRs → **per-concern** passes. For a large PR with several concerns, combine both.

rows.see: accurate but inconsistently explained: the format is already taught, yet single responses drop a different element each time
rows.answer: Add a **self-critique / evaluator-optimizer** step: the agent checks each draft against explicit completeness criteria before presenting. When the required elements are already listed and shown in few-shot examples and single responses still drop a different element each time, more examples don't check the response being sent; a bigger model or a customer-confirmation step doesn't fix incomplete explanation either.

rows.see: resume a multi-agent run without repeating work or losing fidelity
rows.answer: Each agent persists a structured report to a known location; on resume the coordinator loads them and injects relevant state into agent prompts (orchestrator + compact artifact). Not a shared vector store each agent semantic-searches, and not each agent blindly reloading its own file — the coordinator stays in charge.

rows.see: long conversation with transactional data (numbers / dates / IDs)
rows.answer: Pull the facts into a structured block and send it with every prompt. Summarising loses them.

rows.see: “lost in the middle”
rows.answer: Fix the structure. Put the key facts first and add section headers. Do not write 'pay attention'.

rows.see: multiple issues in one session — resolved topics plus one active issue, near the context limit
rows.answer: Extract **structured issue data** (order IDs, amounts, statuses) for each issue into a separate context layer sent with every request. A narrative summary of the resolved issues blurs the numbers the customer asks about later, a sliding window drops the old issues, and re-fetching via tools depends on the agent knowing what to fetch.

rows.see: agent forgets an earlier turn — asks for the name again mid-verification
rows.answer: The API is stateless: resend the full `messages` array on every request. It is not a 2-turn memory default or a missing 'remember' instruction.

rows.see: tool outputs (40+ fields each) now dominate the context
rows.answer: Prune each `tool_result` to the task-relevant fields and drop the rest. A vector DB is overkill; prose summaries throw away the structure you still need.

rows.see: returning customer — an old session's `tool_result` is stale (e.g. `Status: PENDING`) and the agent keeps citing it
rows.answer: Start a fresh session, inject a structured summary of the prior interaction, then make fresh tool calls. Prompting 'prefer the most recent results' or auto re-calling every tool is unreliable.

rows.see: agent cites an old value (a renamed class, an outdated amount) after summarising earlier turns
rows.answer: Progressive summarisation is lossy — it condensed the change into a vague phrase. Not a context overflow and not a stale cached copy; track critical changes in a persistent facts block.

rows.see: early/middle items go vague but the context window is NOT full
rows.answer: Lost-in-the-middle: attention favours the start and end, so middle content degrades. Rule out temperature, sparse source material, and silent summarisation.

rows.see: sliding window dropped an early commitment — agent says 'no record' of a credit or promise made in turn 3
rows.answer: Copy must-survive facts (IDs, amounts, commitments, statuses) into a **structured state object** sent with every request; the window can stay. A bigger window only delays the drop, a summary of the dropped turns blurs the amount, and a transcript-search tool only runs if the agent already knows to look.

rows.see: old turns / tool snapshots are fully superseded and no answer depends on them (e.g. polling a live status every few minutes)
rows.answer: A **sliding window** / clearing old tool results is right: keep the latest few and replace the rest with a placeholder (API tool-result clearing, `clear_tool_uses` with `keep`). A case-facts object or a narrative summary is over-engineering here, and a bigger context window is the antipattern.

rows.see: the customer is frustrated / angry
rows.answer: Mood is not a signal. Escalate only on explicit ones: the customer asks for a human, policy has no answer, or the agent cannot go further.

rows.see: self-reported confidence as an escalation signal
rows.answer: Self-reported confidence is badly calibrated. It is not a valid escalation signal.

rows.see: an explicit human request to escalate
rows.answer: Escalate at once. Do not try to solve it first — no tool calls, no clarifying question before the handoff.

rows.see: an ambiguous customer match
rows.answer: Ask for another identifier. Guessing risks showing the wrong person's data.

rows.see: frustrated customer wants "someone who can help", and the issue is straightforward and resolvable now
rows.answer: Acknowledge the frustration, say it can be completed now, and offer to do it or escalate — escalate if they reiterate. This is the frustration case; an explicit demand for a human is escalated at once.

rows.see: designing the escalation trigger: rules engine vs natural-language criteria vs failure count
rows.answer: Escalation is a judgment call about intent and progress — give the model clear NL criteria (customer asks for a human, issue needs a policy exception, agent can't make meaningful progress). A rigid rules engine, an N-consecutive-failed-calls counter, or a sentiment threshold all miss the long tail.

rows.see: escalation handoff when the human won't see your transcript
rows.answer: Pass a structured summary — customer ID, root cause, amount, recommended action — so the human can act instantly without re-investigating. Not the full transcript, not diagnosis-plus-amount alone, not a DB dump behind a reference ID.

rows.see: escalation calibration is off — escalates easy cases, attempts the hard ones
rows.answer: Root cause is unclear decision boundaries. Add explicit escalation criteria plus few-shot examples to the system prompt first — the proportionate fix, before a trained classifier or a confidence/sentiment router.

rows.see: policy is silent on the request (e.g. competitor price match when only own-site drops are covered)
rows.answer: A genuine policy gap → escalate for interpretation; the agent can't invent policy. Don't confuse it with a multi-issue message (handle sequentially), speculation about future intent, or escalating just to avoid presenting contradictory tracking evidence.

rows.see: a subagent times out / errors
rows.answer: Pass on structured error context: the type, the action, any partial results and the alternatives. Never report empty as success, and never kill the whole pipeline.

rows.see: the action fails but you can still deliver partial value (single agent — e.g. you can explain the charge but `process_refund` times out)
rows.answer: Deliver the partial value, be honest about the failure, and let the user choose escalation or retry later. Graceful degradation — don't falsely confirm success and close, don't loop retries holding the conversation open, don't escalate before giving what you can.

rows.see: some sources/inputs succeeded and others failed (partial upstream data feeding synthesis or a doc pipeline)
rows.answer: Proceed with what you have and mark the output with explicit coverage/gap annotations so downstream and the user see confidence levels. Don't treat partial success as total failure (wastes completed work), don't hide the gaps as if complete, and never fabricate substitute content for the missing parts.

rows.see: a `timeout` and a valid `0 results found` come back from different sources
rows.answer: Distinguish them: a timeout means the data is unknown (retry decision), `0 results` is a successful query that found nothing (accept as a valid finding). Don't lump both as failures (wasteful retries), and don't aggregate into one success-rate metric that destroys the distinction.

rows.see: a subagent returns a generic `"search unavailable"` status
rows.answer: Too coarse: it hides whether the failure is a transient timeout (retry) or a permanent access restriction (switch source), so the coordinator can't pick a recovery strategy. Return the failure type, not a generic message.

rows.see: coordinator is swamped with routine/transient subagent errors
rows.answer: Handle errors at the lowest level able to resolve them: the subagent recovers transient failures locally and propagates only what it can't resolve — with what was attempted and any partial results. Don't push every routine error up, don't mask errors as success, and don't bolt on a pre-validation gate or a separate error-handling agent.

rows.see: context degradation exploring a large codebase
rows.answer: This is an attention problem. Use scratchpad files, subagents for isolation, and state manifests. A bigger window does not fix it.

rows.see: why delegate to a subagent
rows.answer: The main gain is context isolation, not speed.

rows.see: build understanding of a subsystem spanning many files under context limits
rows.answer: Start from the architectural root: analyze imports/class hierarchy to find the base interface, read that, then trace only the specific implementations you need. Do not sequentially Read all files, and do not just size-rank them.

rows.see: context already degraded mid-exploration, need to switch topic
rows.answer: Condense what you learned into a compact summary and give a **fresh** subagent that summary plus the new task. Spawning a subagent but then synthesizing its output back in the already-degraded main context loses the signal you were trying to save.

rows.see: long multi-agent pipeline interrupted — continue without redoing finished units or losing their findings
rows.answer: Each agent writes its structured results to a known location and a **manifest** records each unit's status + output path. On restart the coordinator loads the manifest, skips finished units, reruns unfinished ones, and injects prior findings into new subagent prompts. Not a session/transcript resume (compaction may already have lost detail), not a full rerun, not the coordinator's memory.

rows.see: 97% aggregate accuracy — automate everything?
rows.answer: No. Check accuracy per document type and per field, because one type could sit at 40%. Calibrate on labelled data.

rows.see: which items to send for human review
rows.answer: Use stratified sampling and take the most uncertain items. Not only the low-confidence ones, and not an even spread.

rows.see: route low-confidence extractions to review — but high-confidence ones are still wrong and some low-confidence ones are right
rows.answer: The scores are miscalibrated. Calibrate the thresholds on a labeled validation set so reported confidence tracks real accuracy, at field level not document level. Not: lower the threshold to review everything, or drop confidence scoring.

rows.see: two credible sources conflict
rows.answer: Report both with their source and date, and let the reader decide. Do not just take the newest.

rows.see: different numbers across sources
rows.answer: They may not contradict at all. Different dates explain most of it, so require dates in the output.

rows.see: the synthesis agent paraphrases
rows.answer: Keep the claim to source mapping all the way through. Summarising loses the attribution.

rows.see: generated docs get edited or refactored and no longer say which statement came from which source
rows.answer: Store provenance as machine-readable metadata (source file, line, retrieval date) kept separate from the prose. It survives edits and lets you re-verify only the affected claims. Footnotes, `git blame`, or re-auditing the whole codebase do not preserve claim to source.

rows.see: conflicting findings come out either over-confident or over-hedged
rows.answer: Structure the report to separate well-established from contested claims and keep each source's methodology and confidence interval. Beats picking one arbitrarily, collapsing everything to one confidence score, or filtering out the uncertain findings.

rows.see: document has amendments / superseded values (original vs Amendment 1)
rows.answer: Redesign the schema so amended fields hold multiple values, each with source location and effective date. Beats prompting to always take the newest or preprocessing away the superseded sections.
